**Yes.** The story balances scene and summary well. Dramatized scenes (the breakfast conversation, the dinner over chicken and wine, the closet discovery, the canoe outing) carry the emotional beats through dialogue and action. Summary and exposition do the connecting work:

- the habitual description of the recurring dream
- Daniel's background as an archivist
- the account of how his marriage to Rachel ended
- the compressed "rest of the week passed" transition
- the Delaware Water Gap memory

The exposition is woven into or around scenes rather than piled up. Summary bridges time efficiently, and the story ends in a vivid real-time scene, so the pacing stays engaging and never becomes dry or overwhelming.
